response.title: What battery backup will keep my electric driveway gate working through a day-long power outage?
response.answer:
For a 24-hour power outage, I recommend a LiFePO₄ (lithium iron phosphate) battery backup with roughly 500–1,000 Wh of usable capacity for a typical residential electric driveway gate.

However, the right battery depends on whether your gate uses a 12V/24V DC motor or a 120V AC motor, and how many times you need to open it during the outage.

What size battery do you need?

1,500–2,000+ Wh system

	

Depends on motor and standby consumption

The important consideration is that the gate controller consumes electricity even when the gate isn't moving. Photocells, wireless receivers, keypads and other accessories may also draw power continuously.

For example, a gate controller consuming 15 watts at idle uses:

If you don't know the model, tell me whether it's a sliding gate or swinging gate, and whether it plugs into a normal 120V outlet.

With that information, I can narrow this down to a compatible backup that should keep your gate opening and closing throughout a 24-hour outage, without buying an unnecessarily large battery.

For a **24-hour power outage**, I recommend a **LiFePO₄ (lithium iron phosphate) battery backup with roughly 500–1,000 Wh of usable capacity** for a typical residential electric driveway gate.

However, the right battery depends on whether your gate uses a 12V/24V DC motor or a 120V AC motor, and how many times you need to open it during the outage.

## What size battery do you need?

| Gate setup | Suggested backup | Expected use |
|---|---|---|
| 12V or 24V DC gate | 20–40 Ah battery at 24V | Often sufficient for 24 hours |
| 120V AC gate, light use | 500 Wh power station with UPS capability | May last a day |
| 120V AC gate, regular use | 1,000 Wh power station with UPS capability | Better safety margin |
| Heavy dual gate or high-traffic entrance | 1,500–2,000+ Wh system | Depends on motor and standby consumption |

The important consideration is that **the gate controller consumes electricity even when the gate isn't moving**. Photocells, wireless receivers, keypads and other accessories may also draw power continuously.

For example, a gate controller consuming 15 watts at idle uses:

\[
15\text{ W}\times24\text{ h}=360\text{ Wh}
\]

That is before accounting for motor operation and backup-system losses.

## Battery backups worth considering

For a gate powered from a standard 120V outlet, these are possible options, provided their automatic transfer behavior and motor-starting capacity are compatible.
